 stood out this week as firming crude prices and a wave of expansion news kept the American energy major in the market spotlight, with recent trading reflecting both the pull of rising oil and the company's ambitious plans abroad. The shares have climbed toward record ground during the month as Brent crude strengthened amid shipping worries near the Strait of Hormuz and renewed diplomacy between Washington and Tehran. The recent firmness in oil prices has served as a powerful backdrop for Chevron. As an integrated major with substantial upstream production, the company benefits when the barrel commands more in global markets, and the late-September climb in benchmark crude reinforced that dynamic. Traders watched every twist in the supply narrative, from tanker movements to diplomatic signals, and Chevron absorbed much of that momentum in its daily trading. Firm crude tends to brighten the entire energy complex, and Chevron, as one of the most prominent American names, often leads the way when sentiment turns favorable. The company's blend of oil and gas production, refining, and chemicals means that strength in crude flows through multiple parts of the enterprise, amplifying the effect on the overall picture. Among the most striking developments has been Chevron's plan to deepen its presence in Venezuela, with a multibillion-dollar commitment aimed at expanding crude production in the country over the coming years. The move reflects a willingness to re-engage with a nation that holds enormous reserves, and it has become a defining piece of the company's recent narrative. The plan would roughly double output there, according to reported details, marking a bold frontier bet. Operating in Venezuela carries well-known complexities, from political shifts to sanctions questions, yet Chevron has long maintained a footprint in the country. The renewed push signals confidence that the enterprise can navigate those challenges and extract value from some of the hemisphere's largest reserves. Market watchers have flagged the commitment as a notable divergence from more cautious peers. Chevron has also signaled a marked increase in exploration effort, with plans to lift spending on the hunt for new barrels and to drill a broader slate of exploration wells in the year ahead. The push reflects a belief that fresh discoveries remain essential to sustaining production over the long haul, and it marks a more aggressive stance on frontier acreage than the company has shown in some recent stretches. Ramping exploration is a deliberate wager on replenishing reserves, the lifeblood of any producer. By widening its search across attractive regions, Chevron aims to secure the barrels that will feed its production engine well into the coming decade. The strategy positions the company as one willing to spend on discovery even as it maintains discipline elsewhere. The company outlined its capital plan for the year, striking a balance between funding growth projects and maintaining the financial restraint that the market has come to expect. The budget reflects a measured approach, channeling resources toward high-value developments while keeping a firm grip on overall spending. That equilibrium between ambition and prudence has become a hallmark of how Chevron describes its strategy. Capital discipline matters greatly in a sector prone to dramatic swings. By setting a spending framework that can weather price volatility, Chevron seeks to protect its ability to fund distributions and pursue projects even when crude softens. The plan drew attention as observers gauged how the company would balance its Venezuela ambitions against its broader financial commitments. At home, the Permian Basin remains a cornerstone of Chevron's upstream portfolio. The prolific shale region in the American Southwest delivers a steady stream of barrels, and the company has built a large, efficient operation there. Permian output provides a reliable base of production that complements the enterprise's international ventures, giving it exposure to both onshore shale and offshore megaprojects. The basin's importance extends beyond raw volume. Its short-cycle nature allows producers to adjust activity relatively quickly in response to price signals, offering flexibility that longer-lead offshore projects lack. For Chevron, the Permian serves as both a production workhorse and a lever for managing the pace of spending across cycles. Chevron's footprint spans continents, with major assets ranging from Kazakhstan to Australia and beyond. The company's global reach gives it exposure to diverse sources of oil and gas, from massive liquefied natural gas facilities to sprawling onshore fields. This geographic spread offers a measure of balance, spreading exposure across regions with different cost structures and market dynamics. Managing such a far-flung portfolio requires deep technical and logistical capability, and Chevron leans on decades of engineering experience to develop complex projects. For a retirement-focused investor looking at oil majors today, the choice comes down to Chevron (NYSE:CVX | CVX Price Prediction) versus ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), and the question is simple: Which one deserves the closer look right now for durable oil-patch income? Both are Dividend Aristocrats. Both are throwing off record cash. The differences matter for a retiree who needs the check to keep arriving through the next commodity cycle. Chevron pays more today. At $206.24 a share on Sept. 25, Chevron yields 3.45% on a $1.78 quarterly payout, with an annualized forward dividend of $7.12. Exxon, at $161.67, yields 2.55% on a $1.03 quarterly check and $4.12 annualized. Exxon owns the longer raise record: 43 consecutive years of annual dividend growth versus Chevron’s 39 consecutive annual increases. Both hiked roughly 4% in their latest raises, which puts both firmly in the Dividend Kings conversation (we ranked ten of them by valuation in a free report here). If your priority is the fattest current yield, Chevron wins this round. If your priority is the longest unbroken chain of raises through oil busts, Exxon wins. For a retiree writing checks in 2026, the higher cash yield today edges it: Chevron takes the income round. Chevron trades at a P/E of 32, a P/B of 2.13, and a P/FCF of 24. Exxon trades at a P/E of 23, a P/B of 2.52, and a P/FCF of 28. Exxon’s earnings yield of 4.42% comfortably beats Chevron’s 3.10%, and Exxon posts a higher ROE of 11.03% against Chevron’s 7.26%. Chevron has run harder recently, up 38.84% year to date versus Exxon’s 36.72%, and now trades at a richer multiple as it digests the Hess deal. On the numbers that decide what a retiree is paying per dollar of earnings, Exxon wins valuation. Dividend durability sits in the balance sheet, and the gap here is wide. Exxon carries a debt/equity of 0.17, net debt/EBITDA of 0.55, and interest coverage of 56.3x. Chevron’s figures: debt/equity 0.25, net debt/EBITDA 1.08, and interest coverage 13.7x. Chevron did cut $8.41 billion in total debt in Q2 2026, and management flagged net debt to CFFO of 0.6 times. Exxon’s is simply stronger. Exxon hit record full-year production of 4.7 million oil-equivalent barrels per day, the highest in more than 40 years, with Guyana at roughly 900,000 barrels per day and a fifth FPSO on track for startup by year end. CFO Neil Hansen called Guyana “very much an inflection into free cash flow” and guided to “two times the level of free cash flow in 2030 than we saw in 2025.” Chevron’s record 4,070 MBOED is impressive, but it was driven by the Hess acquisition, which lifted leverage and DD&A. title: Five Energy Stocks Set To Profit As Iran War Drags On (NYSE: CVX, NYSE: COP, NYSE: SHEL, NYSE: LNG, NYSE: MPC) - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By Ewan Scott | Sep 26, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis A prolonged conflict with Iran is opening multiple profit channels across the energy sector, from elevated crude prices to record refining margins, LNG shortages, and extreme shipping costs. Chevron (NYSE: CVX) is among the companies positioned to benefit from sustained higher oil and gas prices as Middle East tensions continue to disrupt global supply chains. ConocoPhillips (NYSE: COP) also offers investors meaningful exposure to elevated commodity prices, though its direct footprint in the Middle East differs from other majors, affecting the degree of disruption risk it carries. Shell (NYSE: SHEL) rounds out the trio of major integrated oil companies seen as well-placed to capitalize on the geopolitical premium now baked into global crude benchmarks. The level of direct Middle East exposure varies considerably across these three producers, meaning the risk profile and upside potential for each company differs in important ways for investors to weigh. Cheniere Energy (NYSE: LNG) stands out as a more direct beneficiary of the supply crunch, given its dominant position in the American liquefied natural gas export market, which has seen demand surge as buyers scramble for non-Middle East supply. Marathon Petroleum (NYSE: MPC) is similarly seen as a direct winner from the current environment, with refining margins climbing sharply as crude flows from the Persian Gulf face increasing uncertainty and disruption. LNG shortages are proving to be one of the most acute consequences of the conflict, as buyers across Europe and Asia move aggressively to secure alternative supply, driving spot prices to elevated levels not seen in recent years. Shipping costs have also reached extreme levels as tanker operators price in the heightened risk of operating near contested waterways, adding another layer of cost pressure throughout the global energy supply chain. The combination of higher crude prices, tightening LNG markets, record refining margins, and surging freight rates is creating a broad and sustained tailwind for energy companies with the right operational and geographic positioning to capture these multiple profit streams. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is set to rule on five closely watched treatments in August from Moderna, Lantheus Holdings, Bristol Myers Squibb, Capricor Therapeutics and Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical. Decisions are due by August 23 at the latest on therapies ranging from an mRNA flu vaccine to a gene therapy for a rare metabolic disorder, putting biotech investors on high alert as the outcomes could drive sharp near-term moves across the sector. Moderna is seeking approval for mRNA-1010, its experimental mRNA-based seasonal flu vaccine for adults 50 and older. An FDA advisory panel already voted unanimously in favor of the shot in June, and the FDA is slated to decide on its application by August 5. The FDA initially refused to file Moderna’s application in early February 2026, citing concerns that the comparator vaccine used in the main trial did not reflect the best available care for older adults. Moderna revised its plan, and now the company is seeking a traditional approval for adults aged 50-64 and an accelerated approval for adults 65 and older. If granted accelerated approval in the patient population, Moderna will be required to conduct another study to confirm effectiveness in the group. Lantheus wants approval for MK-6240, a PET imaging agent that detects tau protein tangles in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. Doctors would use the scan to help confirm the presence of tau pathology, stage the disease, and guide treatment decisions. The FDA accepted the company’s application seeking approval in October and granted it a fast-track designation. The application is based on two late-stage trials in people with early Alzheimer’s disease. In both trials, the scan identified patients with tau pathology and ruled out people without it, to support the application. The FDA will decide on the application by August 13 at the latest. Bristol Myers Squibb is seeking approval for iberdomide, an oral drug combined with existing medicines for patients whose multiple myeloma has returned or stopped responding, by August 17. It works by helping the immune system attack cancer cells more effectively while also directly killing myeloma cells. Bristol Myers’ application was accepted by the FDA in February and granted priority review. The application relies on the large late-stage trial where iberdomide, together with Daratumumab and Dexamethasone, showed a statistically significant improvement in minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity rates compared to control arms. MRD negativity means no detectable cancer cells remain after treatment — an early sign of deep response. Capricor is seeking full approval for Deramiocel, a cell therapy aimed at heart damage caused by Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After an earlier rejection, the company submitted new data from its late-stage HOPE-3 trial to the FDA. However, in July, an advisory committee voted 9–3 against the claim that the available evidence provides substantial proof of effectiveness for treating DMD cardiomyopathy. The vote is non-binding, meaning the FDA could still approve the therapy. Ultragenyx is seeking approval for DTX401, a one-time gene therapy for glycogen storage disease type Ia, a rare inherited metabolic disorder, by August 23. People with GSDIa cannot release stored sugar from the liver, leading to dangerous drops in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) during fasting, excess glycogen buildup in the liver and kidneys, and other long-term complications. The FDA granted priority review to Ultragenyx’s application in February. There are currently no approved treatments that address the underlying cause of GSDIa. Omeros Corporation said on Monday that U.S. Medicare officials have approved extra payments to hospitals that use its newly launched drug YARTEMLEA to treat a rare and often deadly complication of stem cell transplants. Shares of the company were trading 4% higher at the time of writing. Starting October 1, hospitals can receive up to about $287,000 more from Medicare for each qualifying patient under the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ new status for the therapy. The extra funds go straight to the hospitals to help cover the high cost of the new treatment. Omeros itself will still receive the same payment for the drug. YARTEMLEA is the only medicine approved in the United States for this transplant complication, known as TA-TMA. The condition damages small blood vessels and can be life-threatening, especially for the kidneys. About three in 10 patients who receive the more complex type of stem-cell transplant in the U.S. are covered by Medicare. Company CEO Gregory Demopulos said the decision should make it easier for hospitals to choose the drug based on what patients need, rather than worrying about the cost. YARTEMLEA reached the market earlier this year after winning FDA approval in late 2025. It is Omeros’ first commercial product and the main source of near-term revenue. The company is counting on growing sales of the drug to help fund the rest of its research pipeline, which includes longer-lasting versions of similar medicines, experimental cancer therapies, a potential treatment for cocaine addiction, and other programs aimed at hard-to-treat conditions. title: Chevron's Cost Discipline: Turning Efficiency Into Lasting Value - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation’s CVX recent quarterly performance highlights one aspect of its strategy that deserves particular attention: structural cost reduction. Rather than relying solely on higher commodity prices to improve profitability, the company has been working to lower the underlying cost of running its operations. Chevron achieved $3 billion in annual run-rate structural cost reductions since 2024, reaching its target six months ahead of schedule, and it also targets $3-$4 billion of structural cost reductions by the end of 2026. Management noted that more than 70% of these savings came from efficiency improvements, an important distinction because operational efficiencies can provide benefits that persist beyond short-term spending cuts. The impact is particularly visible in Chevron’s shale operations. The company expects to spend 25% less capital per barrel of oil equivalent in 2026 compared with 2025. CVX also achieved savings that have largely offset inflationary pressures while allowing the company to continue growing production across key assets, including the Permian, Gulf of America and Guyana. Technology and operational changes are supporting this efficiency push. Chevron’s cost-reduction efforts include portfolio optimization, greater use of technology to enhance productivity and changes in how and where work is performed, including expanded use of global capability centers. The broader significance is resilience. Energy prices inevitably fluctuate, but a structurally lower cost base can help Chevron remain competitive across commodity cycles. By combining disciplined spending with operational improvements, the company is creating a business capable of generating more value from its existing assets rather than depending entirely on higher production or favorable oil prices. Other Energy Peers That Follow Cost Reduction Strategy Cost efficiency has become an important competitive battleground for major oil companies, and Chevron is not alone in this strategic program. A few other energy companies are also following the same. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM continues to make strong progress on its structural cost-saving program, aimed at offsetting inflation and the higher operating expenses associated with growth. XOM has generated $16.3 billion in cumulative structural cost savings since 2019 and targets $20 billion by 2030. Savings have primarily come from business transformation, greater end-to-end accountability and consolidation of centralized organizations. The newly formed global operations organization is expected to unlock additional efficiencies by spreading best practices across the portfolio. ExxonMobil is also developing an enterprise-wide ERP system that could further improve efficiency. Despite inflation and significant business growth, the company expects to keep cash costs broadly flat, highlighting the effectiveness of its cost discipline. Shell plc SHEL is making strong progress on its structural cost reduction program, with $700 million in savings delivered so far in 2026. The company’s broader $5 billion-$7 billion target is already about halfway achieved, ahead of schedule. Shell’s initiative goes beyond simply cutting expenses and focuses on enhancing free cash flow by improving asset reliability and availability, strengthening business models, turning around underperforming operations and creating a leaner, more focused organization. Management sees additional opportunities and is pushing toward the upper end of the target range. Shell also plans to use AI and efficiency benchmarks to unlock further value, making cost discipline an ongoing cultural transformation rather than a one-time savings exercise. NYSE Composite drew fresh attention on Wednesday as the integrated energy major featured prominently in coverage of a firmer crude backdrop, a widely reported multi-year commitment to expand Venezuelan crude production, and continued discussion of the company's planned capital budget for the coming year. Trading in the name unfolded against a market where energy sat squarely in focus, even as broad US indices came under pressure from rising Treasury yields and renewed inflation concern. The combination of a headline-grabbing overseas expansion and a steady spending framework kept Chevron among the more closely watched energy majors during the session. The integrated oil and gas segment spans exploration, production, refining, chemicals, and marketing, and Chevron ranks among the largest operators spanning that full chain. Firms of this scale tend to move with the rhythm of crude and natural gas pricing, refining margins, and the cost of capital that funds long-cycle projects. During the current stretch, crude prices firmed on reports of shipping disruption tied to the Strait of Hormuz, lifting sentiment across the group. At the same time, elevated bond yields raised the discount applied to distant cash flows, tempering enthusiasm for capital-intensive names. Chevron sits at the intersection of those forces, with a diversified asset base that spreads exposure across geographies and product streams. That breadth has historically helped the company absorb swings in any single region, though it also ties performance to the wider commodity cycle that governs the entire sector. Chevron operates upstream assets across the Permian Basin, the Gulf of Mexico, Kazakhstan, Australia, and a growing roster of international positions, alongside downstream refining and a substantial chemicals joint venture. The Permian remains a central engine, prized for its flexibility and relatively short cycle times, which allow output to be dialed up or moderated as pricing shifts. Management has emphasised capital discipline, directing spending toward assets that generate cash efficiently while restraining the pace of expansion elsewhere. The company's integrated structure means refining and chemicals can cushion periods of softer crude, since those units often benefit from lower feedstock costs. Chevron's operational focus in recent reporting centred on wringing efficiency from existing acreage and advancing a handful of large projects that are meant to sustain production over a multi-year horizon, a stance that fits the broader industry move toward measured growth rather than aggressive drilling. The most prominent recent development involved a widely reported plan to channel substantial capital into Venezuela over the coming years, aimed at roughly doubling crude production the company draws from that country. Coverage framed the commitment as a notable re-engagement with a region that carries both resource depth and a complicated operating history. Separately, Chevron was reported to be advancing partnership discussions tied to Vietnamese energy demand, part of a wider push to widen its international footprint. Reporting also noted efforts to expand the gas portfolio through positions in Argentina and the Mediterranean. Each of these threads points to a company willing to pursue selective growth abroad even as it holds spending discipline at home, a balance that featured heavily in how commentators described the name during the session. Across the wider energy complex, movement among oil and gas stocks reflected the pull between firm crude pricing and the pressure that higher borrowing costs placed on capital-heavy producers, a tension that shaped trading sentiment through the session. Chevron has outlined a spending framework for the coming year that keeps capital within a defined band, signalling continuity rather than a sharp acceleration. The approach reflects a preference across the major producers to fund distributions and steady project execution while avoiding the boom-and-bust spending patterns that marked earlier cycles. By anchoring the budget within a stated range, management aims to give the market a clear read on how cash generated at prevailing prices is likely to be deployed. The framework covers upstream development, downstream maintenance, and lower-carbon initiatives, and it sits alongside the company's stated aim of sustaining its dividend, long a defining feature of the name. Observers noted that a disciplined budget can steady sentiment when crude swings, since it limits the degree to which spending balloons during price spikes and contracts during downturns. Trading unfolded within a market where rising Treasury yields, firm inflation readings, and expectations of further central-bank action weighed on richly valued corners of the market, particularly technology. Energy, by contrast, drew support from firmer crude, creating a rotation dynamic that favoured producers on some sessions. For a name like Chevron, the environment cut both ways: stronger crude lifted the revenue backdrop, while higher discount rates pressured the present value of long-dated projects. The push and pull left the stock sensitive to each fresh data point on prices, yields, and geopolitics. Commentators described the setup as one where macro forces mattered as much as company-specific news, a reminder that even a diversified major remains tethered to the broader financial climate that governs how capital flows into and out of the energy complex. Across the wider industry, executives voiced concern about tightening global fuel supply, with some warning of strain in refined products even as crude drew geopolitical support. Shipping disruption near key chokepoints added a premium to seaborne barrels, sharpening focus on producers with flexible output. The period also saw continued discussion of how majors balance traditional hydrocarbon development against lower-carbon commitments, an ongoing theme that shapes capital allocation across the group. Chevron featured in this conversation given its scale and its stated aim of growing both conventional production and select lower-carbon lines. Chevron's scale, dividend history, and index membership make it a reference point for how the energy majors are faring within the S&P 500. Chevron Corporation CVX reportedly plans to begin seismic research in blocks off Greece by the end of this year, marking an important step toward assessing the region's hydrocarbon potential. The energy major is expanding its offshore exploration footprint in Greece, strengthening its position in the Eastern Mediterranean. Chevron's country manager Beatrice Bienvenu, during a meeting with Greek energy minister Stavros Papastavrou in New York, indicated that seismic research in the Ionian Sea and areas south of the Peloponnese and Crete will begin by year-end. Chevron has been steadily building its presence in Greece. Earlier this year, the company acquired a 70% stake from Helleniq Energy in an offshore block southwest of the Ionian Sea. A Chevron-led consortium also secured exclusive lease agreements to explore for natural gas across three additional deep-sea blocks off the Peloponnese and Crete. Chevron and Helleniq Energy's agreements cover four offshore blocks — South Crete 1, South Crete 2, South of Peloponnese and Block A2. Together, these areas span approximately 47,000 square kilometers, creating a sizable exploration position in the Eastern Mediterranean. The planned seismic research represents an initial step rather than an immediate move toward commercial production. Seismic exploration will help Chevron and its partner better understand the geological characteristics and potential hydrocarbon resources beneath these offshore areas before decisions on test drilling are made. The joint venture has outlined a three-phase exploration program covering seismic data acquisition, exploratory drilling and reservoir analysis. This process is designed to determine whether commercially viable oil and natural gas resources exist within the offshore acreage. Chevron's growing presence may also support Greece's ambitions in the Eastern Mediterranean energy market. Greece's location near Europe, the Middle East and North Africa gives the country strategic importance as it seeks to expand domestic hydrocarbon development and strengthen its position in regional energy markets. The document notes that Greek energy minister Papastavrou views these developments as important for national energy security and domestic hydrocarbon production. The Chevron-Helleniq projects are also expected to support employment, technology transfers and broader industrial activity within Greece's energy sector. For Chevron, Greece adds another component to an already established Eastern Mediterranean portfolio. The company has active natural gas fields in Israel as well as interests in Egypt and Cyprus, giving CVX an existing operational presence across the region. The Eastern Mediterranean remains an important part of Chevron's future energy portfolio, while Greece's undeveloped resource potential provides another exploration avenue. The planned seismic campaign therefore extends CVX's regional footprint while laying the groundwork for determining whether the Greek offshore blocks can eventually support commercially viable development. Chevron is one of the largest publicly traded oil and gas companies, with operations that span almost every corner of the globe. Currently, CVX carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). title: CVX vs. TTE: Which Energy Major Has the Stronger LNG Growth Story? - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX and TotalEnergies SE TTE are two major integrated energy companies with significant oil and natural gas operations. Both are benefiting from a supportive commodity-price environment, but their LNG strategies provide an interesting basis for comparison. Chevron is expanding its natural gas and LNG portfolio while benefiting from strong production growth following the Hess acquisition. TotalEnergies, meanwhile, already has a large global LNG business and is pursuing additional projects to expand its position across the LNG value chain. With energy security becoming increasingly important and global LNG demand continuing to grow, investors may be wondering which energy major offers the stronger combination of growth, valuation and earnings momentum. Let's dive deep and closely compare the fundamentals of both stocks to determine which one is a better investment now. Chevron's Production Growth Strengthens Its LNG Story Chevron delivered a strong second quarter, with earnings of $12.1 billion and adjusted earnings of $12 billion. Worldwide production increased 20% year over year to 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, while U.S. production reached a record level. The company also achieved $3 billion in annualized structural cost savings and $1.5 billion in annualized Hess-related synergies. The Hess acquisition has significantly strengthened Chevron's production profile, particularly through its interest in Guyana's Stabroek Block. Management expects production to continue growing, supported by Guyana, the Permian Basin, Kazakhstan and other projects. Chevron is also becoming more aggressive in LNG. The company expects to have about 20 million metric tons per annum (Mtpa) of LNG supply capacity, including 16 Mtpa of net gas production from its projects and 4 Mtpa of contracted U.S. Gulf Coast supply. Chevron is also evaluating additional opportunities in Argentina, the Eastern Mediterranean, Australia and Africa. The push reflects growing demand for diversified and reliable gas supplies. TotalEnergies brings a more established LNG platform to the comparison. The company sold 44 million tons of LNG in 2025 and describes itself as the world's third-largest LNG player. It expects LNG volumes from equity production and long-term third-party purchases to increase 50% between 2025 and 2030. The company is continuing to add projects to its portfolio. In July, TotalEnergies shipped the first LNG cargo from the ECA LNG project in Mexico and will offtake 1.7 million tons per year for 20 years once commercial operations begin. TotalEnergies also approved development of the Cronos gas field in Cyprus, with production expected to start in 2028. The project is designed to supply European markets through existing LNG infrastructure in Egypt. These developments give TotalEnergies substantial exposure to the LNG growth opportunity, while its integrated model also provides exposure to oil, refining, trading and electricity. Chevron vs. TotalEnergies: Which Stock Has the Lower P/E? Valuation is one area where the two stocks show a notable difference. Based on the data, Chevron trades at a forward P/E of 13.35X, compared with 8.46X for TotalEnergies. Chevron's higher multiple reflects its strong production growth, Hess-related synergies and high-quality upstream assets. However, TotalEnergies offers investors exposure to a substantial LNG business at a considerably lower earnings multiple. The valuation gap is also consistent with recent peer data showing TotalEnergies trading below Chevron on forward earnings multiples. TotalEnergies Leads Chevron in One-Year Stock Performance TotalEnergies has outperformed Chevron over the past year. The chart shows TTE's share price gaining 48.8%, compared with a 30.7% increase for CVX. TotalEnergies' performance reflects investor interest in its integrated energy model, LNG exposure and capital returns. TTE reported second-quarter adjusted net income of $6 billion and cash flow of $9.8 billion, while its gearing ratio declined to 13%. Chevron, meanwhile, continues to benefit from strong operating momentum. Its second-quarter cash flow from operations reached $22.6 billion, compared with $8.6 billion in the year-ago quarter. Over the past 60 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate trend for CVX's third-quarter 2026 earnings has increased 18.98%, while the fourth-quarter estimate has risen 20.83%. Meanwhile, the consensus estimates for fiscal 2026 and 2027 have increased 11.55% and 12.16%, respectively. In comparison, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for TTE's third-quarter 2026 earnings has increased 9.72%, while the fourth-quarter estimate has risen 31.12%. The consensus estimates for fiscal 2026 and 2027 have increased 6.69% and 11.74%, respectively. The stronger upward revisions for Chevron coincide with its recent production growth, cost reductions and improved earnings performance. TotalEnergies has also recorded positive estimate revisions across all four periods, although the increases were smaller in three of the four periods. Both energy majors have compelling LNG growth stories. Chevron offers rapidly growing production, Hess-related synergies and an expanding LNG portfolio. TotalEnergies brings a much larger established LNG business, a broader global portfolio and a substantially lower valuation. The data also show stronger one-year share-price performance for TotalEnergies, while Chevron has delivered more pronounced upward earnings estimate revisions. TotalEnergies carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), while Chevron has a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). content: Shares of Chevron experienced a 1.4% uptick on Wednesday, peaking at $207.00 during intraday trading before closing around $205.21. The session witnessed more than 8.2 million shares exchanged. Trading volume registered a 23% decline compared to the typical daily average of approximately 10.7 million shares. The previous trading day concluded with shares at $202.41. Analyst sentiment toward the energy behemoth remains predominantly positive. The Street consensus shows a “Moderate Buy” rating alongside a mean price objective of $211.35. Among the more optimistic assessments, Piper Sandler elevated its price target from $207.00 to $243.00 earlier this month. Additional recent coverage from Jefferies and Sanford C. Bernstein included buy ratings and market perform designations respectively. During a Tuesday evening appearance at a WSJ Leadership Institute dinner held in New York, Chevron’s CFO Eimear Bonner outlined expectations for continued elevated energy prices. She cited ongoing disruptions to shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz and limited refining capacity as key factors. Brent crude experienced a 1% decline on Tuesday, settling just below the $100 per barrel threshold. Bonner emphasized that Chevron’s strategic priority centers on optimizing supply output while maintaining operational reliability across its refining operations. The CFO also provided updates on Chevron’s Venezuelan operations. Earlier this month, the company announced a $7 billion commitment to develop the country’s oil reserves through three separate joint ventures spanning five years. However, Bonner tempered expectations by noting Venezuela won’t contribute significantly to new supply in the immediate future. Looking ahead, Chevron has outlined plans for an approximately 50% surge in exploration capital expenditures for next year. This aggressive drilling campaign aims to bolster future production capacity and reserve levels. Additionally, Greece’s energy ministry confirmed that Chevron will commence seismic research activities in offshore exploration blocks before the year concludes, expanding the company’s geographical exploration footprint. Chevron delivered better-than-anticipated results in its most recent quarterly earnings release on July 31st. The oil giant reported earnings per share of $6.06, surpassing the consensus forecast of $5.55. Quarterly revenue totaled $67.20 billion, significantly exceeding analyst projections of $62.72 billion. This represented a substantial 57.4% year-over-year increase compared to the corresponding quarter. The company maintains a quarterly dividend distribution of $1.78 per share, translating to an annualized yield of 3.5%. The current payout ratio registers at 68.26%. On a less favorable note, corporate insiders have divested more than 1.15 million shares valued at approximately $225.9 million during the past three months. Notable transactions included substantial sales by CEO Michael Wirth and board member John Hess. Regulatory uncertainty also looms with the proposed Diesel Price Reduction Act of 2026, which could impose temporary limitations on diesel exports when domestic prices exceed $5 per gallon. The legislation currently has minimal congressional support. Chevron’s current market capitalization approaches $405.45 billion, accompanied by a price-to-earnings ratio of 19.68. Technical indicators show the 50-day moving average positioned at $200.25, while the 200-day moving average rests at $191.97.
